lesson.title: Breaking Numbers Down to Their Building Blocks
lesson.summary: Prime factorization rewrites any whole number greater than 1 as a unique product of prime numbers, the same building-block idea that later drives finding greatest common factors, simplifying radicals, and factoring polynomials.
lesson.body:
Every whole number greater than 1 is either prime or built out of primes. A prime number, like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, or 13, has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself. A composite number has more than two factors, which means it can always be broken down into smaller pieces. The number 1 is a special case: it is neither prime nor composite, since it has only one factor, itself. Prime factorization is the process of breaking a composite number down completely until only prime numbers remain in the product. Because primes cannot be split any further, they act as the "atoms" of multiplication, the smallest pieces every number is built from, the same way atoms are the smallest pieces ordinary matter is built from.

The most common method is a factor tree. Start with the number and split it into any two factors, prime or not. Circle any prime factors you land on, and keep splitting any composite factors until every branch ends in a prime. A second method, repeated division, divides the number by the smallest prime that fits evenly, then repeats on the quotient until the quotient itself is 1. It does not matter which two factors you choose to start the split, since every complete path through the tree eventually lands on the same set of primes.

Consider 360. Divide by 2: 360 divided by 2 is 180. Divide by 2 again: 180 divided by 2 is 90. Divide by 2 a third time: 90 divided by 2 is 45. Now 45 is odd, so move to the next prime, 3: 45 divided by 3 is 15. Divide by 3 again: 15 divided by 3 is 5. Finally, 5 is itself prime, so 5 divided by 5 is 1 and the process stops. Collecting every divisor used gives 360 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5, which is usually written with exponents as 2^3 x 3^2 x 5. To check the work, multiply back: 2^3 = 8, 3^2 = 9, and 8 x 9 x 5 = 72 x 5 = 360. The factorization checks out.

This connects directly to the idea of Number itself. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that every whole number greater than 1 has exactly one prime factorization, aside from the order the factors are written in. That uniqueness is what makes prime factorization useful rather than just a curiosity: whether you start splitting 360 as 36 x 10 or as 8 x 45, every path through the factor tree eventually lands on exactly the same result, 2^3 x 3^2 x 5. No other combination of primes multiplies to 360.

Prime factorization is not just an isolated skill. It is the tool used to find the greatest common factor and least common multiple of two numbers, to simplify square roots such as writing the square root of 72 as 6 times the square root of 2, and, later, to factor polynomials by pulling out common numeric factors before dealing with the variable parts. Learning to break a number down into primes now is exactly the same instinct algebra will ask for when breaking an expression down into its simplest factors.

A common mistake is stopping too early, for example writing 360 = 4 x 9 x 10 and calling it done. Each of those factors, 4, 9, and 10, is still composite, so the factorization is incomplete until every factor is prime. A quick way to check a finished factorization is to make sure every number in the product appears on a basic list of primes, 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, and so on, and that multiplying every listed factor back together returns the original number.
